05-rsi-extremes.easy_to_get: S — gives the correct, deflationary definition of RSI ('recent up-moves have been much larger than recent down-moves, nothing more') and then the thesis: the same reading means three different things in three regimes.

Part 2's honesty note about unknowable institutional parameters

06-moving-averages.delivers: A — was C, and this was the real defect. One objective claimed crossovers are lagging with '60-80% of move already done' while the body says 20-30% in eleven places, including the arithmetic that derives it and the quiz answer that tests it. Another promised the reader would apply the Pilot Line, which the lesson never explained. A third said 'trade pullbacks TO moving averages' under a title reading Stop Buying the Touch. All three now match the lesson underneath them.
06-moving-averages.easy_to_follow: A — was B. Builds well: myth, then what MAs actually show, then why algos react anyway, then the Golden Cross arithmetic, then the event framework. 06-moving-averages.easy_to_get: S — the hook is a timestamped 40 seconds (10:18 touch, 10:22 through it, stop gone) and then the claim in plain words: a 50-period EMA is the average of the last fifty closes, no order sits at that number. Title, hook and Part 1 all argue the same thing.
06-moving-averages.evidence: A — was B. The composite's win rate went to counts (16 of 45). The bare '60-70%' algo share now says it is an industry estimate that moves with venue and instrument — which this lesson, three sections from its own model caveat, had no excuse not to do. And 'acting on TD alone = getting faked out 50% of the time' is replaced by what TD actually claims: selling looks exhausted, which is not the same as the reversal having started.
strengths: The Golden Cross lag is derived from the arithmetic, not asserted

The retail-belief vs reality split is concrete and hard to misread
Explains why MAs sometimes 'work' (clustered algo behaviour) without conceding they are support

06-moving-averages.worth_the_time: S — the Golden Cross section is the best thing in the beginner tier. It does not assert the lag, it derives it: a 50-bar average has to cross a 200-bar average, so price must have risen for weeks first. And its stat box carries the caveat the rest of the corpus should copy — 'these are working figures, not a published study … check the lag yourself on the instrument you actually trade.'

07-revenge-trading.delivers: S — four objectives, four delivered, nothing major taught that no objective mentions.
07-revenge-trading.easy_to_follow: S — the strongest build in the tier. Cascade (loss aversion → cortisol → prefrontal shutdown → the trade), then the three tilts, then the case, then the four circuit breakers, then daily prep. Every term is defined before it is relied on, and the case study is placed after the mechanism it illustrates rather than before it.
07-revenge-trading.easy_to_get: S — opens in second person on the thing itself ('you're opening another trade. Bigger size this time. No setup. No plan. Just rage.') and then names the claim in two sentences: this isn't a discipline problem, it's a neuroscience problem. Nothing in the lesson pulls against that.
07-revenge-trading.evidence: S — the best-evidenced lesson so far, and the only correction needed was one rounding slip. Loss aversion is attributed to Kahneman and Tversky by name, given as roughly 2:1, and explicitly hedged: 'the exact ratio varies by person and context, but the asymmetry itself is well established.' The case study's arithmetic reconciles at every step — the running P&L chain (340, 1,580, 6,260, 15,180, 23,400), the 69x multiplier, the $17,140 the three-strike rule saves, the $16,400 the loss limit saves, and the 3x size costing $1,240 where 1x costs about $410. The cooldown argument is checked against the case study's own timestamps: 26, 29 and 29 minutes between trades, so three of the four fall inside a thirty-minute cooldown. Only the drawdown was wrong — $23,400 on $350,000 is 6.7%, not 6.8% — and it is now right.
strengths: The circuit breakers are distinguished by what each limits, not just listed
Every one carries a 'without willpower' version, which the neuroscience section makes necessary
The cooldown claim is tested against the case study's own timestamps rather than asserted
Loss aversion is named, sourced and hedged in one sentence
Winner's tilt and boredom tilt are genuinely useful additions — most treatments only cover revenge
weaknesses: 'Marcus entered all 4 revenge trades at emotional state 2-3' appears only in the Quick Wins, as a self-report the case study never recorded — harmless, but it is the one number in the lesson that is not derived from something stated earlier
07-revenge-trading.worth_the_time: S — the four circuit breakers are separated by what each one actually limits, which is the non-obvious part: the strike count caps how many times you can be wrong, the loss limit caps what each of those times may cost, the cooldown caps how fast they arrive, and the size lock caps the acceleration. Most treatments of this topic list the same four rules without ever saying why you need more than one. Each also carries a 'making it work without willpower' step, which follows directly from the neuroscience the lesson opened with.

08-confirmation-bias.easy_to_follow: A — builds well: what it is, three ways it shows up, the echo chamber that amplifies it, falsification as the counter, the red-team drill, then systems, then the case study last. CVD and HTF both arrive un-expanded in the Real Example, but both were introduced earlier in the tier (lessons 2-3 and 6), so this is a reminder problem rather than a forward reference.
08-confirmation-bias.easy_to_get: S — the opening is the cleanest statement of the idea in the corpus: you and your friend look at the same candle and see opposite things. The claim lands in four sentences and the lesson never drifts from it.
08-confirmation-bias.evidence: A — was C, and this was the whole of the gap. The worst of it was the BTC $45k head-to-head, where the retail trader is stopped for -$500 and the professional skips the trade AND re-enters lower AND makes +$1,300. The professional wins twice, by construction, in an example built to let him. What that teaches is that falsification pays; the honest claim is narrower and more useful, and the lesson makes it elsewhere ('the trades you DON'T take will save your account'). The outcome now says so directly: you are not buying a better hit rate, you are buying the ability to state before entry what would make you wrong. Also fixed: '10x worse' (a multiplier with nothing behind it), a feed that is '100% bullish, 0% bearish' (hyperbole printed as a finding, in a lesson about mistaking certainty for evidence), and Alex's -$2,200 counterfactual, which reconciles with none of the tranches the case study describes — on equal shares the loss at $285 is about $1,100, on equal dollars about $1,000.
strengths: The opening states the idea in four sentences with no jargon
The invalidation step in the red-team checklist is the part most treatments omit
Trap #1 catches hindsight bias specifically, which is usually conflated with confirmation bias
Systems-over-willpower is carried forward correctly from lesson 07
weaknesses: The echo-chamber part is a full section on a widely known point, and is the least dense stretch of the lesson
'30% win rate' in the selective-memory example is illustrative and flagged as such, but it is still a number doing rhetorical work
08-confirmation-bias.worth_the_time: A — the red-team checklist is genuinely actionable and the invalidation step ('at what price is the bull case DEAD?') is the part most treatments leave out. The three objectivity systems are practical. The echo-chamber section is the weakest: correct, but the point is widely known and the lesson spends a full part on it.

09-position-sizing.delivers: S — four objectives, four delivered, including the one most sizing lessons skip: when the right size is zero.
09-position-sizing.easy_to_follow: A — expectancy, then fixed fractional, then ATR, then portfolio heat, then the checklist, then the mistakes. Each part needs only what came before.
09-position-sizing.easy_to_get: S — 'You have a 60% win rate. Your friend has 40%. Who makes more money?' is the whole lesson in three sentences, and the expectancy table right after it settles the question with arithmetic rather than assertion.
09-position-sizing.evidence: A — was B, and the problem was a contradiction rather than a fabrication. Part 2 stated the rule as 'never risk more than 1% on a single trade' and Parts 3, 5 and 6 then sized A-grade setups at 2%, with a quiz asking why flat 1% is 'amateur hour'. In a risk lesson aimed at beginners that is the sentence most likely to be acted on, and the page said both things. It now reads '1% on a single trade, and never more than 2% however good the setup looks', and the quiz asks what flat sizing gives up rather than calling it amateur. The explanation now says plainly that until your own journal shows your grades separate your outcomes, flat 1% is the correct size and not a beginner's mistake — which is what the lesson's own practice exercise already concedes. Also: 'makes almost 3x per trade' compared +$140 with -$50, which is not a multiple of anything; 'even A-grade setups fail 30-40% of the time' was an invented rate; and Mike's counterfactual quietly dropped the trade he won, so it is now stated with the winner included.
strengths: Expectancy is derived with two worked traders, not asserted
Mike's cascade is arithmetically exact at every step, including the 10%-of-current-balance compounding
The drawdown-recovery table (10 needs 11.1, 20 needs 25, 50 needs 100) is correct and rarely shown
The practice exercise refuses to predict the reader's result and says why
weaknesses: Grading setups A/B/C is introduced as though the reader can already do it reliably; the exercise later admits they probably cannot
09-position-sizing.worth_the_time: A — the drawdown-recovery arithmetic in Mistake #5 is the part most beginners have never seen stated (a 20% loss needs a 25% gain, a 50% loss needs 100%), and every figure in it checks out.

10-stop-losses.delivers: A — four objectives, four delivered. Breakeven-at-1R and never-widening are both covered.
10-stop-losses.easy_to_follow: A — percentage stops fail, then ATR for how far, then structure for where, then the 2R rule, then a six-step placement procedure. 'ATR tells you HOW FAR. Structure tells you WHERE' is the cleanest sentence in the tier.
10-stop-losses.easy_to_get: S — the hook is the exact experience the lesson is about: stopped at 2%, then a 10% rally without you. The claim ('the market has no idea what 2% of your account is') is the thesis and never wavers.
10-stop-losses.evidence: A — was C, and this lesson needed the most repair of any so far. Three things. First, a quiz was grammatically broken: 'You observe at $100 ... Where often your stop be?' and 'Stop placement often be structure-based' — what an automated should-to-often hedging pass leaves behind when it hits a modal verb. This is the only lesson in the corpus where that pass broke the grammar, and it broke the question a beginner is asked to answer. Second, the 2R quiz illustrated a 40% win rate with '4 losses + 6 wins', which is 60%, and claimed you need '60%+ accuracy' below 2R when at 1:1 you need 50%. Third and largest, a six-method comparison table reported stop-out rate, false-stop rate, average loss, win rate and expectancy 'based on Kevin's 8-month testing' — but the case study says Kevin traded three methods and settled on a fourth. The 1.5x and 3.0x rows were measurements of an experiment that never happened, under a heading reading 'What The Data Shows'. The five invented columns are gone; the methods and their use cases remain, because Part 2 already derives that comparison honestly. The recovery phase's +91% and its supporting statistics went too.
strengths: 'ATR tells you HOW FAR. Structure tells you WHERE' organises the whole lesson in eight words
The break-even hit rate is derived per ratio rather than asserted
Step 4 makes stop distance an input and size an output, and says so explicitly
Sarah's stop-moving sequence is short, concrete and arithmetically exact
weaknesses: Kevin's case study is long — 622 words — and its three phases restate a point Part 1 has already made
The remaining phase statistics for the two failed methods are still composite figures; they are kept because a disaster record illustrates a mistake rather than claiming a return
10-stop-losses.worth_the_time: S — the 2R section derives the break-even hit rate at each ratio (1:1 needs 50%, 2:1 needs 33%, 3:1 needs 25%) instead of asserting a rule, and the six-step procedure makes stop distance an input and position size an output, which is the actual inversion most traders never make.

11-timeframe-illusion.easy_to_follow: A — addiction trap, then the mechanism, then the alignment framework, then timeframe by account size, then costs, then the matrix. HTF/MTF/LTF are expanded on first use.
11-timeframe-illusion.easy_to_get: S — the best hook in the tier. Same instrument, same moment: the 5-minute chart shows a clean breakout, the daily shows a lower high three days into a downtrend. 'Both charts are right ... on a 5-minute chart you are looking at a keyhole.' Then the structural claim: 390 bars against 1 is not 390 times the insight, it is 390 times as many moments in which you can talk yourself into a trade.
11-timeframe-illusion.evidence: A — was D, and this was the sharpest self-contradiction in the corpus. Part 1 contains the best caveat anywhere in these 82 lessons: 'no public dataset cleanly measures retail returns by timeframe, so treat any precise figure quoted for this — here or anywhere else — as invented.' The matrix in Part 5 repeats it. Part 2 was then a precise figure for retail returns by timeframe: Jessica turning -$18,300 a year into +$46,116, a 145.5% annual return, off a timeframe change; Tom's recovery quantified to the dollar; three-year projections; and a burnout table giving the percentage who quit. The Key Takeaways headed the pair 'Real examples prove the pattern' and added 'Pattern repeats across thousands of traders' — twice — which is exactly the population claim the lesson had already said nobody can make. All of it is gone. The behavioural changes stay, because they are what a reader can copy and they are not claims about what the method earns: 3,355 trades against 52, 1,560 hours against 120, and a commission bill that fell with the count.
strengths: The Part 1 caveat is the model the whole corpus should follow, and it is now the only kind of claim the lesson makes
The keyhole image does more work than any statistic could
'Higher timeframes do not have a better win rate. They give you fewer chances to be wrong, and charge you less each time you are' is the honest version of the thesis
Smaller-account-means-higher-timeframe is counterintuitive, correct, and derived from cost as a share of capital
weaknesses: Two composite traders still carry the emotional weight of Parts 1 and 2; they now illustrate rather than prove, but the lesson would lose nothing by being shorter
11-timeframe-illusion.worth_the_time: S — the argument is structural rather than statistical and says so: more bars means more decisions, your error rate per decision does not fall because there are more of them, every decision pays a spread, and the cost scales with frequency while your edge does not. That survives being asked where it came from.

12-paper-trading.easy_to_follow: A — the illusion, then the three-stage system, then what paper can and cannot teach. Each stage carries its own goal, duration and graduation criteria, so the reader always knows which one they are in.
12-paper-trading.easy_to_get: S — the hook is four numbers and one sentence: 87 paper trades, 55%, up 16.7%, then down 40.5% live on the same strategy — 'a person who has never lost real money has not yet met the person who will be placing their orders.'
12-paper-trading.evidence: A — was C. The lesson cited a study that does not exist: 'Based on Mark's experience + aggregate data from 800+ traders (2021-2024)' headed the three-stage table, and the table then reported that study's win rates by stage. Everything downstream inherited it — 'win rate drops 7-17% from paper to live', '80% who skip Stage 2 blow up within 90 days: average loss -$4,800 to -$8,200', 'expect 15-25% performance drop', and a quiz whose correct answer was one of the invented percentages. All of it is gone. The win-rate column is now qualitative and says why, and where the shape of a claim is right but its size unknowable, the text says the size is unknown. What the lesson keeps is stronger: Mark does not lose win rate so much as the ability to follow his own checklist, 100% to 32%, and that is a mechanism a reader recognises without needing a survey. The lesson had also already got one thing right that most of the corpus got wrong — it explicitly separates the $6,080 that left the account from the $4,800 he never made, 'a different kind of expensive'.
strengths: The distinction between what paper CAN and CANNOT teach is the cleanest framing of this topic anywhere
Already separated realised loss from opportunity cost before this audit, and said why that matters
The five gaps are concrete and each names a behaviour, not a number
Graduation criteria are checkable by the reader without any external claim
weaknesses: The 'What SHOULD have happened' micro-account projection is still a month-by-month curve for something that did not happen; it is written in the conditional throughout, which is why it stays, but it is the least evidenced block left in the lesson
12-paper-trading.worth_the_time: A — the paper/micro/standard progression is the actionable core, and the reason for the middle stage is argued rather than asserted: the lessons arrive either way, and the only thing you control is what they cost.

13-smart-money-concepts.delivers: S — four objectives, four delivered, including the one that matters most: why the vast majority of order-block candidates on a chart are not valid ones.
13-smart-money-concepts.easy_to_follow: A — was B. Order blocks, then the three requirements, then breaker blocks, then BOS/ChoCH, then the two combined setups. 'Displacement' was the word the whole lesson turns on — it appears in Rachel's framework, in Mistake #4 and in the comparison table — and Requirement #1 described it without ever naming it. It is now named where it is defined.
13-smart-money-concepts.easy_to_get: A — 'Support and resistance are where retail traders think price will react. Order blocks are where institutions actually entered' states the distinction in two sentences and the lesson holds to it.
13-smart-money-concepts.evidence: A — the table opens by refusing to print win rates ('we have not run a study that would let us fill them in honestly, and neither has anyone whose numbers you will find quoted elsewhere') and its last row then printed one: 'Below 50% win rate = negative expectancy'. That contradicted the table's own header, and the claim is separately false — expectancy depends on the payoff as well as the hit rate, which lesson 09 demonstrates with a trader who wins 40% and makes money. A reader who did both lessons would have had to decide which to disbelieve. The row now says what is actually wrong with a retail support line: nothing has to happen for one to exist except that price was there before. Also hedged: '50-70% fill typical' for fair value gaps, a measured-sounding figure nobody measured.
strengths: The frequency column, and the argument that rarity is the point rather than a drawback
Refuses win-rate columns explicitly and says why
The breaker-block mechanism is explained through trapped positioning, not asserted as 'more powerful'
The house analogy for a breaker block is the clearest in the corpus
weaknesses: Four Signal Pilot products appear in the two setup checklists; each is cross-linked, but this is a dense product moment for lesson 13
13-smart-money-concepts.worth_the_time: S — the comparison table with its frequency column is the best teaching device in the tier, and the 'How to read that table' section is why: 'frequency is a warning, not a feature'. A retail support line appears fifty times a month because the only thing required to draw one is that price has been there before; a breaker block appears two to four times because three separate things have to happen in order. Each row down the table removes a way of being wrong.

14-cot-report.delivers: S — four objectives, four delivered, including the reporting-lag question that most treatments of COT either ignore or get wrong.
14-cot-report.easy_to_follow: A — what it is, then the three groups, then the three metrics, then the case study, then extremes, then divergence, then the framework. The COT Index formula is given before the percentile thresholds that depend on it.
14-cot-report.easy_to_get: A — the hook is concrete and checkable: institutional positioning, published free every Friday by the CFTC, and most traders ignore it. The three-group structure (commercials, non-commercials, small specs) lands immediately.
14-cot-report.evidence: A — this lesson already carried three of the best caveats in the whole curriculum before I read it: on the commercials, 'that does not make them right, and there is no honest number we can put on how often they are'; on the participant table, no accuracy column because 'nobody has published a study that would settle it, and the figures circulating online trace back to nothing'; on the thresholds table, a reversal-probability column removed for the same reason. Then Metric #2 said 'They're RARELY wrong at extremes' and 'a mean reversion is coming', and the retail section said small speculators are 'consistently wrong at extremes' — precisely the claims those three notes forbid. Both now state the mechanism instead: an extreme is where positioning cannot go much further, and a crowd at an extreme has already acted. 'The Holy Grail Setup' and 'this is where COT becomes LETHAL' are gone too — they sold certainty about the one technique Part 4 spends its length insisting is only a bias. Arithmetic: $2,185 to $2,045 is $140 an ounce, not the $150 stated, and $140 on two 100-ounce contracts is exactly the $28,000 the same paragraph gives.
strengths: Three caveats that refuse to invent an accuracy figure, and say why the ones circulating online cannot be trusted
The bias-versus-timing distinction, stated as a wrong-way/right-way pair
The 2008 crude oil example is real, checkable, and correctly quoted ($147 to $33, -77%)
'What alignment buys you: not a probability, but four independent reasons instead of one' — the honest version of a confluence claim
weaknesses: The hook promises you can see where institutions are positioned 'before the market moves', which is a stronger claim than the lesson's own bias-not-timing framing supports
The 'How to read them' blocks still translate positioning directly into 'price is likely topping', which Part 1's own key insight walks back two paragraphs later
14-cot-report.worth_the_time: S — teaches a real, free, public data source and, more importantly, the right way to hold it: 'COT gives you the bias, technicals give you the timing.' The wrong-way/right-way pair is the clearest statement of that distinction in the corpus, and Part 4 is built entirely around not trading the signal on its own.

15-liquidity-pools.easy_to_follow: S — pools, then why they get hunted, then the four types, then inducement, then three-drive, then the framework, then the case, then the table. The mechanism is given before any of the patterns that depend on it.
15-liquidity-pools.easy_to_get: S — 'Support and resistance aren't walls, they're liquidity pools where institutions hunt your stops before making their real move' is the thesis, stated in the first four lines, and the lesson never departs from it.
15-liquidity-pools.evidence: A — and the gap was internal. The comparison table had already had its sweep-probability and reversal-rate columns removed, with a note saying so: 'we had a figure against each one and cannot show you where those figures came from, so they should not have been there.' The case study underneath then reported a 100% hunt rate — 31 out of 31 consecutive trades, every one reversing to her exact target — and a recovery quantified as an 8% hunt rate, 65% win rate, +$37K and +71%, with an alternative approach winning 78% of the time against 0%. None of that survives the standard the table sets three screens later. The case now describes the shape, which is what makes the point: a wick just past her level, then a reversal towards the target she had picked, in the same form each time. Her own closing line was always the strongest thing in the section and needed no help from the figures — 'my stops were not unlucky, they were predictable ... you are findable.'
strengths: Explains why sweeps happen from the institution's execution problem, not from malice
The table's own note on why its probability columns were removed
Distinguishes the sweep from the reversal — two events, not one
'A moving average is not a liquidity pool. It moves every candle' — a category error named as one
Amanda's closing line does the work the statistics were doing, better
weaknesses: 'Average sweep distance $0.28 beyond stop' is a suspiciously exact figure for a composite, though it is at least the right order of magnitude for the instruments named
15-liquidity-pools.worth_the_time: S — the reason institutions sweep is explained rather than asserted: a fund that wants 10,000 contracts cannot market-buy them without paying for the privilege, so it sources the other side where the other side is already resting. And the 'How to read that table' section is the best analytical writing in the corpus so far: 'more touches means more stops, and that is the whole mechanism'; 'getting swept and reversing afterwards are two different events'; and on moving averages, 'it moves every candle — stops do not follow it, they sit at fixed prices', which it correctly calls a category error rather than a weak setup.

16-market-structure-advanced.easy_to_follow: A — displacement, then mitigation, then OTE, then the two checklists. The order-block versus mitigation-block distinction is made explicitly ('order blocks are for INITIAL entries, mitigation blocks are for ADDING to winners'), which is the confusion this material usually leaves in place.
16-market-structure-advanced.easy_to_get: A — 'Price moves $10 in 20 minutes. No pullbacks. That's not retail buying' states the idea before naming it, which is the right order for a term as jargon-heavy as displacement.
16-market-structure-advanced.evidence: A — was C, and this was the starkest contradiction I have found. The comparison table removes two columns and explains why: 'it used to carry a follow-through rate and an average move for each one, attributed to thousands of tracked setups. We cannot show you that dataset, so those two columns are gone.' The block immediately beneath it, headed 'What The Data Shows', then reprints every one of those numbers as a finding — 78% and 2.8R for displacement + OTE, 68-72% for BOS, 54-58% for CHoCH, 62-68% failure for counter-trend, 58-62% and 1.3R for fair value gaps. Same screen, opposite claims. All seven bullets rewritten to say what the ordering actually rests on, which the lesson establishes well elsewhere. The confluence bullet is the one that improves most: it used to promise a higher hit rate and now says what confluence really buys — not certainty but room, because the more elements that land on the same price, the tighter the stop that still sits beyond all of them. Ryan's before-and-after win rates and +68% recovery are gone too; what replaced them is the actual finding, that his read of direction was already right and only his standing point was wrong.
strengths: 'Why OTE Works' explains a Fibonacci level as self-fulfilling rather than natural, and says that is the better reason
Order block versus mitigation block distinguished by purpose, not by shape
The layered-entry technique is concrete and correctly reasoned
The table's own note about the removed columns was already right — the problem was the block that ignored it
weaknesses: Displacement is defined as '5-7+ consecutive candles' throughout, which is firmer than the concept warrants; the same move on a different timeframe is a different candle count
16-market-structure-advanced.worth_the_time: S — 'Why OTE Works' is the best paragraph in the intermediate tier and possibly the corpus. It states that 61.8% is the golden ratio and 78.6% its square root, that nothing about the market obliges price to respect either, and that what makes them work is that they are on every charting platform by default so a very large number of participants are watching the same two prices. Then the line that earns it: 'the level is self-fulfilling, not natural, and that is a better reason to use it than mysticism would be.'

17-time-sales-mastery.easy_to_follow: S — what the tape is, then what counts as large, then the three signals, then aggressive versus passive, then the fingerprints. The instrument-by-instrument size table arrives before any threshold depends on it, which matters because '1,000 contracts' means nothing without knowing 1,000 of what.
17-time-sales-mastery.easy_to_get: S — 'Candlesticks show you WHAT happened. Time & Sales shows you WHO did it and WHY' is the whole lesson in one line, and it holds up under the rest of it.
17-time-sales-mastery.evidence: A — the analysis is honest and the quiz explanations were not. Three of them handed the reader a trade that wins by construction: Lisa taking five consecutive 2,000-lot buys for +15 points, a reader entering at 4,551 'BEFORE the breakout candle closes' and running to 4,565, and — as the final line of the entire lesson — 'this is Lisa's edge that turned her account from -$16K to +$38K', a figure that appears nowhere else and contradicts her own case study, which is six weeks of losses with no recovery figure attached. Two smaller ones in the body: five tape prints meaning 'price is about to move higher', and the tape reader beating the candlestick reader by a stated $2.00. All now say what the tape actually establishes, which is narrow and useful: somebody with size is in a hurry. Whether they are right is a separate question, and the tape does not answer it. The quiz-3 rewrite makes the honest version of the claim — what the tape buys you is time, not certainty.
strengths: The aggressor-versus-size bullet is the single best sentence about order flow in the corpus
Size thresholds are given per instrument rather than as one number
The three fingerprints are distinguishable from each other, which most treatments fail at
The premium-setup box already refused to quote a win rate and argued from independence instead
weaknesses: 'The 5-10 minute rule' is presented as a rule when it is a heuristic nobody has measured; it is at least framed as an observation about follow-through rather than a probability
17-time-sales-mastery.worth_the_time: S — the 'What The Tape Tells You' bullets are among the best analytical writing in the corpus. That an iceberg is one order fed out in slices rather than a coincidence. That a thousand contracts lifting the ask and a thousand filled passively on the bid are the same quantity and opposite information — 'one of them paid the spread to get in now, and that is the part worth reading'. And that three prints in a row is a different event from one big print, because a single large buy can be a hedge, a roll or a rebalance, while three lifting the offer is a campaign.

fixed: The clock contradicted itself four ways. The Asian range was quoted as 6 PM-2 AM, 7 PM-3 AM, 7 PM-2:30 AM and 7 PM-4 AM in different sections, and the kill zone as 2-5 AM in the headings but 3-5 AM in the checklist and workflow. Settled on one scheme — the range you MARK is 7 PM-2 AM, the kill zone is 2-5 AM everywhere — and added a short 'note on the clock' in Phase 1 explaining why the marked range is narrower than Tokyo's session hours: a high printed at 3 AM was made inside the sweep window, so it is something the sweep produced, not something it is aiming at.

The composite carried an after-record: 'His 9:30-11 AM trades had 61% win rate.' A win rate for a session window, attributed to an invented account — and on the same page as a table that says win rates attributed to unshowable data were removed. Replaced with 'Same setups, same rules, worse hours', which is the actual lesson.

Jason's closing quote was truncated mid-sentence ('same strategy, Session timing is everything') — collateral from the earlier arc-sentence sweep. Rewritten to a whole thought that names the mechanism: he stopped paying the spread on moves with no one behind them.

Quiz Q2's explanation ended with a constructed win: 'You shorted the sweep reversal at $4,558 for +23 points.' The worked example is fine; the fill is invented. Replaced with what the range actually gives you — two levels worth watching and a reason to be at the screen when one breaks.

'Every. Single. Day.' in the hero and 'This happens DAILY' in Part 1 both contradicted the lesson's own closing caveat that no session pattern is owed to you. Both rewritten to describe the shape rather than promise the frequency, with the sit-out skill named explicitly.

Three unevidenced rankings in the comparison table: 'HIGHEST probability' for the kill zone row, 'Trade in London direction for highest %', and 'All strategies work best here'. Replaced with what the row can actually support — the setup's name, 'trade London's direction until NY rejects it', and 'deepest order book of the day'. The 'High-Probability NY Reversal Entry' heading became 'The NY Reversal Entry Checklist'.
18-session-liquidity-advanced.kept: Jason's disaster numbers (168 trades, 38%, -$31,200, 23% in the dead zone) stay — a composite may illustrate a mistake, and these claim nothing about what the reader will earn. The table's own note about the removed win-rate columns stays as written.
18-session-liquidity-advanced.notes: After the fix this is the beginner tier's strongest reference lesson. The remaining soft spot is that the Asian-sweep cycle is asserted rather than measured — but the lesson now says so twice, in Part 1 and in the takeaways, instead of only in the takeaways.
18-session-liquidity-advanced.summary: A genuinely useful lesson about *when* to trade, built on a four-phase cycle that is easy to hold in the head: Asia builds the range, London sweeps it, New York confirms or rejects, the afternoon fades. The three LKZ patterns are worked with consistent arithmetic (15-point risk, 35- and 55-point targets, 2.33R and 3.67R — all correct), the daily workflow is a real checklist, and the seven-row session table is the best reference artefact in the beginner tier. Jason's dead-zone story is the right kind of composite: it illustrates a mistake (72 trades in the 6-8 AM chop) and names the mechanism, without claiming what the fix earns.

fixed: Derek's composite carried the full after-record the corpus rule forbids: '$36,660 → $61,200 (+67%), 43 trades, 35 winners' with an 81% win rate — and it sat four screens above a table whose own header says the win-rate column was removed because the dataset cannot be produced. The caveat beside it did not fix that; it just made the page argue with itself. Replaced with what the checklist demonstrably did: rejected 28 setups he would previously have taken, with no way to know how those would have gone.

'ANY rule prevents 5-8 losses, ALL rules = $0 lost' is a backtest fitted to the same twelve trades it was derived from — exactly the overfitting the curriculum warns about elsewhere. Kept the counts, added the admission: the rules were written after looking at these twelve losses, so of course they catch these twelve, which makes them a hypothesis to test forward rather than a result.

The NQ worked example ended with a constructed outcome ('dropped 15,480 → 15,310 over next 6 hours, 170-point move'). The ES example above it states no outcome at all, so the pair was inconsistent as well as invented. Replaced with the sequence the example actually teaches — divergence, then structure break, then entry with the stop above the failed high — and the note that no worked example can tell you whether a given one followed through, which is why there is a stop.

The delta interpretation bands (+1000 = strong, ±300 = balanced) were given with no instrument or timeframe attached, so a reader would apply ES 5-minute numbers to a 1-minute chart or a stock. Added the scaling note: +1000 is enormous on a bar that trades 2,000 contracts and unremarkable on one that trades 40,000, so calibrate the bands to what a typical bar in your instrument actually prints.

Two direct contradictions inside the flagship example. The footprint table labelled the +2,100 row '🔥 STRONG BUY' while the surrounding prose calls that same level a trap and 'light buying at top' — relabelled 'Aggressive buying', which is what the numbers show without endorsing it, and rewrote the prose to compare the two sides in contracts (5,900 hit the bid below, 3,700 lifted the offer above) so the reader can check it.

The pattern table's Reliability column read 'Low' on both exhaustion rows while the same rows recommend a fade — ambiguous about what is low. Now 'Low as a bullish signal' and 'Low as a bearish signal'.
19-footprint-charts-advanced.kept: Derek's loss record (12 trades, 0 winners, -$28,340, and the three named losers) stays: a composite may illustrate a mistake. The 'trust the footprint — not because it is never wrong' line stays as one of the better caveats in the corpus.
19-footprint-charts-advanced.notes: At 4,097 words this is the longest beginner lesson and it earns the length. The residual weakness is that reliability ratings across the nine-row table are editorial judgements presented in a column that looks measured; the table's own header now says no win rates are claimed, which is the honest framing available.
19-footprint-charts-advanced.summary: The best on-ramp in the corpus. A reader who has never seen a footprint chart gets a 30-second explainer, a side-by-side 'same bar, two stories' comparison, and then a worked footprint table whose arithmetic is exact — the five per-level deltas sum to the stated -1,400 and the five level volumes sum to the stated 11,800. That internal consistency is rare and it is what makes the trap example land. Parts 2-4 build cleanly: imbalance → stacked imbalance → absorption vs exhaustion (with the four-way context grid that is the real content of the lesson) → POC migration → divergence. The nine-row pattern table at the end is a genuine reference. Both worked examples state entry, stop and targets before anything else.

fixed: The Marcus-versus-Aisha comparison was the corpus's worst constructed win: two invented traders, same stock, same three weeks, with a stated '$8,170 performance gap', Marcus at 0 wins from 3 and Aisha at 2 from 2 — presented as proof that 'understanding institutional behavior is the entire edge', four screens from a table that says its win-rate columns were removed because the dataset cannot be shown. Rewritten to keep the pedagogy and drop the scoreboard: each side now describes where its rules take it, and the closing note says outright that a composite can be written so whichever side the author prefers comes out ahead, and names the four decisions where the approaches actually diverge.

Monica's composite carried a '+37% Recovery After Fix' stat box and a '$64K → $88K' arc. Removed. The fix paragraph now states what the sizing rule actually buys — at a quarter of the size, the same META gap costs $1,200 instead of $4,800 — and says explicitly that a sizing rule is a claim about how large your worst day may be, not a claim about returns.

Twenty-one blocks of dead .quiz-feedback markup across nine lessons (20, 56, 57, 58, 59, 60, 61, 75, 78). The enhanced quiz script wipes and rewrites that container on first click, so the text never reaches a reader — but it was still in the HTML, still being translated into eleven languages, and in this lesson it duplicated every explanation and carried invented figures ('saved $5,150', 'saved $3,180', 'would have saved $14,850' — a number that does not even reconcile with the $27,710 loss it claims to reduce). All 21 removed; markup verified balanced across all 82 lessons.

Three incompatible holding periods: 'holds 2-7 days' in the summary, 'hold times extend to 5-20 days' in the Real Talk box, and 2-14 days across the comparison table. Settled on the table's ranges and pointed the summary at it.

Two pieces of unearned hype: 'a single trade can run 10-30% while you sleep' and 'But the edge? Massive.' Replaced with what is actually true of the timeframe — a position has room to work over days, and speed stops being the deciding factor.

The AAPL example was headed 'Real Example' while the TSLA one above it is labelled illustrative, and its own numbers disagreed: Target 2 listed at $255 but the outcome line said $252. Relabelled to match, reconciled to $255 (+11.8%, 1:3.4), and added the line that matters — if it stops first, -$8, which is the only one of the two numbers you control. The TSLA card's entry and R:R were likewise brought into line with the body text above it.

The journalling rule said 'adjust if win rate <50% or payoff ratio <2:1' — which contradicts lesson 09's expectancy teaching, since 40% at 3:1 is a working system. Now expectancy-based, with the instruction to read the two numbers together and an example of each direction.

Two quiz explanations were arithmetic on invented data ('same gaps cost $7K instead of $27K') or an invented statistic ('earnings are 50/50'). Both rewritten to the mechanism: the gap you cannot control versus the multiplier you can, and structure telling you nothing about what a company will report.

The tier-completion card and the 'Next: Intermediate Tier' pointer sat between the two quiz blocks, so the lesson congratulated the reader on finishing before quizzing them five more times. Both moved after the final quiz.
20-swing-trading-framework.kept: Monica's mistake record (2% sizing, 5 of 8 trades gapped, TSLA -$2,950 against $738 intended, $92K → $64K) stays: a composite may illustrate a mistake. The TSLA scale-out arithmetic stays as a worked calculation — it is the reader following the maths, not a claim about outcomes.
20-swing-trading-framework.notes: Two quiz blocks totalling eight questions is still more than any other lesson, but with the celebration moved to the end the order at least reads correctly. Worth revisiting if the tier-closing pattern is ever standardised.
20-swing-trading-framework.summary: The tier's closing lesson and the one that carries the most weight: it has to convince a reader who has spent nineteen lessons on intraday mechanics that the daily chart is a different game, and it does. The strongest sections are the four institutional traps (each one a mechanism, not a warning), the daily-order-block explanation grounded in why a fund cannot buy 50,000 shares in one order, and the position-sizing argument, which is the best-argued idea in the beginner tier: a stop is an instruction to sell at a price, a gap means that price never trades, so the only lever you hold is the multiplier in front of it. The scaling arithmetic is exact — the SPY average entry of $592.20 and the TSLA 2.96R both check out to the cent.

fixed: Nina's composite still carried a recovery arc — a 'Final $142K' stat box and 'Account recovered $83K → $142K in 5 months' in the case-study answer. Removed. The answer now says what the fix removes (a cost paid 18 times a day whether she was right or wrong) rather than what it earned.

'Limit orders only — roughly 60% of the spread saved' was an efficacy figure with nothing behind it, repeated in the quiz explanation. Replaced with the mechanism: on a limit order she is quoting rather than paying, so the spread stops being a cost charged at every entry.

The practice exercise was confirmation bias by design. Its success metric was 'find 3-5 instances where spread widening preceded price movement', which can only ever confirm the signal. Rewritten to demand a count rather than a collection: log every widening including the ones followed by nothing, two columns, and finish able to say 'N times, M of them moved'. The note that a signal firing eleven times and preceding a move four times is still useful — but only if you know it is four out of eleven — is the point the exercise now teaches.

'Spread changes predict price changes' stated as fact. Replaced with what is actually happening (a market maker repricing risk, often before the risk reaches price) plus the failure modes the exercise then makes the reader count: a quote server hiccup, one participant stepping away, the tail of an auction.

The hero asserted '$3,000 this year' as a fact about the reader. The arithmetic is right but belongs to a stated size and frequency, so it now carries them: $3,000 at fifty trades a month on a $10,000 position, with the instruction to work out your own.

'If the spread is over 0.1%, you're not trading—you're gambling' and 'high-probability entry' in the confluence box — both replaced with what can be supported: above 0.1% the spread is doing more to the result than the entry, and the confluence setup is three independent things agreeing rather than one.
21-bid-ask-spread-dynamics.kept: Nina's disaster record (1,620 trades, 61%, -$41K gross and -$41K in spread, $165K → $83K) stays, and so does the sentence that makes it land: the spread did not turn a winner into a loser, it doubled a loser. The <10%-of-stop rule stays, now labelled a rule of thumb, because the lesson derives the real break-even arithmetic beside it.
21-bid-ask-spread-dynamics.notes: The only remaining soft spot is the Step 3 table mapping spread width to a maximum number of trades per day; those counts are editorial judgement presented in the same visual register as the derived arithmetic elsewhere on the page.
21-bid-ask-spread-dynamics.summary: The best-argued lesson in the corpus so far, and the one whose arithmetic holds up under the closest reading. Its central move is to convert an invisible cost into a break-even win rate the reader can check: a 1-point stop with a 0.25-point spread needs 62.5% at 1:1, and the lesson says 63%; Nina's $25 spread against a $75 stop needs 66.7%, and the lesson says 67%. Both derivations are correct, and both are the kind of number a reader can verify with a pen. The internal consistency of the composite is equally rare: 1,620 trades at $25 is $40,500, quoted as $41K; week 8's 90 trades at $25 is exactly the $2,250 stated. The reframing of the spread as a tax on impatience rather than a fee, and of market makers as being paid for your urgency, is the clearest explanation of microstructure cost in the curriculum.

fixed: The composite carried a complete after-record — a 'Gained $41K in 8 weeks (44% recovery)' line in the header, a results block quoting 21 trades at 71% for +$41,200 and $93,000 → $134,200, a '+44.3%' ROI line, the section heading 'Jake's Transformation', and individual winning trades (+$2,850, +$3,620). All removed. What replaces it is the one thing about the recovery that can actually be checked: the filter halved his entry count, 21 trades against 34, and a rule whose main effect is to subtract entries has no P&L to report for the entries it subtracted.

Two invented statistics. 'Order book = theater — 80% is noise, 20% is real money' in the takeaways contradicted the lesson's own hero, which honestly says some of it is real and nothing on screen labels which; and the closing line congratulated the reader on reading the book 'like the 5% who actually profit from it', a figure of the same family as the 90%-of-traders-lose myth that lesson 62 spends a section debunking. Both replaced.

Both trading strategies were labelled 'Expectancy: Positive' — a claim about what a setup earns, with nothing behind it, in a curriculum that elsewhere teaches expectancy is something a journal reports. Now each states its R:R (a property of where you put the stop and target) and says outright that expectancy is what your own records tell you after twenty or more.

The case-study quiz actively dismissed the sizing problem: option D ('too large position sizes') is marked wrong, and the explanation never mentions that Jake was putting $18K-$35K of 0DTE options on an account that had fallen to $93K. A reader could finish the lesson believing the sizing was fine. The answer now concedes D is wrong only as an answer to the question asked — the analysis produced the entries — while naming the sizing as a second, separate disaster, and notes that fixing the analysis while keeping the sizing fixes half a problem.

The practice exercise's success metrics asked the reader to 'find 2-3 spoofing instances, 2-3 absorption patterns, 1-2 exhaustion patterns' — a specification that can only be met by collecting confirmations. Rewritten to a tally: every logged wall goes into exactly one of three columns, and the proportions across all ten or more are the output. Collecting only the interesting walls measures nothing.
'Result: High-probability long setup' in the imbalance section, in a lesson whose whole argument is that no single order book reading is worth acting on alone.
22-order-book-analysis.kept: Jake's disaster half stays in full — the three named trades, the per-phase win rates (21%, 17%, 13%), the running balances, and his journal entry, which is the most honest paragraph in the case study. His closing advice stays under a heading that no longer calls it a transformation.
22-order-book-analysis.notes: The 'absorbs 5,000+ shares = real' threshold is instrument-specific and stated flatly; it works as a rule of thumb for the liquid names the lesson uses but would mislead on a thin one. Worth a scale note if this lesson is revisited, of the kind added to lesson 19's delta bands.
22-order-book-analysis.summary: The single most useful distinction in the microstructure sequence, taught cleanly: the order book shows intentions, which can be cancelled, and only a tested level shows anything real. Everything downstream follows from that — absorption versus exhaustion as the same setup with opposite outcomes, the three iceberg detection methods (refreshing, volume exceeding visible size, price stickiness), and spoofing identified by what a fake wall does rather than by how big it is. Jake's disaster is the best-constructed cautionary record in the corpus: three phases summing exactly to the stated -$72,000, running balances that reconcile at every step ($165K → $136.6K → $104.7K → $93K), and 34 trades with 6 wins matching the quoted 17%.

fixed: 'Real Example: Tesla Stop Hunt (September 2024)' was the corpus's most serious fabrication: a minute-by-minute account with timestamps, share counts and low prints, presented as a recorded event, on a date when TSLA was not trading anywhere near the quoted $242. Relabelled as an illustrative reconstruction, the date and ticker attribution removed, and the reader told directly to treat any minute-by-minute account of a sweep — here or anywhere else — as a diagram rather than as evidence.

Inside that example, two invented figures derived from the invented data: '~$15-20M of stop liquidity based on volume profile' and 'estimated profit for hunt orchestrators: $125K-$420K in 45 minutes'. The first is replaced with the honest statement that stop liquidity is unknowable from outside — which is exactly why it is worth so much to whoever can see it — and the second with the economic point that survives without numbers: the buyer is buying from people who are not choosing to sell.

'How Janus Atlas users traded this: Result: +1.1% gain while stopped-out traders lost -1%' — a product efficacy claim built on a fabricated tape. Replaced with the setup's actual content: where the entry sits, where the stop sits, and $1.40 per share at risk at a level that has just proven it can be broken.

'The pattern repeats every single day across thousands of instruments' — replaced with the version that is true and more useful: common enough to learn, not a rule, and plenty of breaks below support are just breaks below support. Janus Atlas marks the sweeps; it cannot tell you which reverse, which is why the entry waits for the reclaim.

'Stop hunts aren't manipulation—they're automated liquidity provision' is a legal characterisation the lesson is not in a position to make, and it sits oddly beside the same lesson's 'dirty tricks' and 'maximum carnage'. Now: whether a given sweep crosses that line is for a regulator with the order records; what matters to you is that none of it is aimed at you personally and all of it is aimed at where predictable stops sit.
'Total liquidity: $10M+ in guaranteed sell orders' — stops are not guaranteed anything, as lesson 20 spends a section establishing. Now 'a pool of forced sell orders — not chosen, just triggered'.

Two slippage figures stated as results ('$0.08 → $0.01/share', repeated in the quiz). Replaced with the structural fact: a limit order cannot fill worse than its limit, so the slippage line goes to nothing on the fills you get and the cost moves to the fills you don't.

An after-record hiding inside the case-study answer, which the earlier corpus sweep missed because it was mid-paragraph: 'Results: stop hunt rate 12/month → 1/month, recovered +$51K.' Removed, with the observation that replaces it — three of the four rebuild rules make his stop harder to find and none make him faster.
23-market-making-hft.kept: Carlos's disaster record in full, including the three named hunts and the note that the later ones cost more because he sized up to make the earlier ones back — a detail that does more work than the totals do.
23-market-making-hft.notes: Evidence graded B rather than A: the lesson's factual spine (rebate economics, co-location, IEX's speed bump) is sound, but the '~50% of US equity volume' figure and the maker-taker rates are quoted without a source. Also fixed the checker rather than the text for Turkish 'dakika dakika', which is a legitimate reduplication of the same kind as 'adım adım' and was already in sanity.py's allowlist for its siblings.
23-market-making-hft.summary: The lesson that reframes the whole microstructure sequence: you are not being cheated, you are being modelled, and the fix is not speed. Part 1 is its best work — three revenue streams with the arithmetic shown ($0.05 × 1M shares × 250 days = $12.5M; $0.0015 rebate × 1M × 250 = $375K), which converts an abstraction into a business you can see yourself funding. The stop-hunt economics in Part 3 are the clearest statement in the corpus of why stops cluster where they do and why that clustering is worth money to someone. Carlos's disaster reconciles exactly: $68,200 in hunts at ~$1,450 across 47 events, plus $5,800 of slippage, equals the stated $74,000, and $155K less that is the stated $81K.

fixed: The footprint anatomy table did not reconcile with the candle printed above it. The eight price levels sum to 15,250 contracts; the candle was labelled 10,000. This is the flagship demonstration of the lesson and the one table a careful reader would add up — lesson 19's equivalent sums exactly. Corrected to 15,250 and the reader now invited to check it.

Jordan's after-record ran through five separate places: a '+$9,980 in total' heading, four winning trades with P&L, a 'four trades, four winners' box, a '$19,000 swing' follow-up, an empty 'Jordan's Complete Transformation' card, and 'This distinction turned 6 consecutive losses into 100% winners'. All removed. The six post-fix decisions are now listed as decisions — what the footprint said and what he did — with no outcomes, and the box that used to hold the result now says where the evidence actually lives: in the six autopsies, not in the four entries.

Two counterfactual savings — 'Skipped, saved -$1,240 loss' and 'avoided $980 loss', totalled as 'saved $2,220'. A trade not taken has no result, and these claimed to know one. Replaced with the general statement, which the lesson is now in a position to make: any lesson that tells you a skipped trade saved a specific number is inventing it.

26-smart-money-divergence.summary: A well-organised lesson with one genuinely excellent section that most of the corpus lacks: 'Common Divergence Mistakes' concedes, unprompted, that a single divergence can persist for weeks in a strong trend, that divergences against the higher-timeframe trend usually produce consolidation rather than reversal, and that a divergence without a trigger is an invitation to sit in drawdown. That is three real limitations stated plainly, and it is why the framework that follows — minimum two divergences, plus a structural trigger — is worth following. The four divergence types are cleanly separated by what data each one reads, and the quiz arithmetic checks out (120K→50K is the stated 58%, +8,500→+2,000 the stated 76%).

fixed: The practice exercise ended: 'After 10 trades, compare expectancy of 3/3 alignment vs 1/3 alignment. The data will prove the framework works.' That is an exercise designed to confirm its own lesson, at a sample size that cannot settle anything, scoring only the trades the reader took. Rewritten with both problems named: ten trades will be mostly noise, and if you only score what you entered you have thrown away the comparison group — so log the 1/3 setups you skipped and what they did.

Seven probability claims. 27-multi-timeframe-mastery.notes: The three alignment tiers now describe evidence rather than odds, but they still rank setups, which is the correct thing for this framework to do — three independent readings agreeing genuinely is more evidence than one. The change is that the lesson no longer converts that into an implied hit rate.
27-multi-timeframe-mastery.summary: The most cleanly structured lesson in the tier. The core idea — HTF for bias, MTF for structure, LTF for timing, and never let a timeframe do a job it cannot see — is stated once and then held consistently through a four-step workflow, a five-step execution table, three alignment tiers, a scaling-in ladder and a scaling-out ladder. The arithmetic is exact throughout: the worked SPY setup's $5.50 over $1.50 is the stated 3.67R, and the pyramid's weighted average entry (50% at $512.50, 25% at $514.20, 25% at $516.50) is the stated $513.90 to the cent. Alex's disaster is the right kind of composite: the failure mode is named as blindness rather than bad luck, and the quote admits the prior year's success was accidental alignment with a trend he did not know existed.

fixed: 'This setup has 75-80% win rate historically' — the most explicit fabricated statistic found in the audit so far, sitting in a quiz answer. Removed and replaced with the reason it cannot be quoted: nobody has measured this setup across a sample worth the name, and a figure invented for a lesson is worse than no figure. What survives is the checkable part — four independent things had to agree, and if the stop goes they were all wrong together.

The three framework-ranking sentences were each attached to the block BEFORE the framework they describe: 'Why this one ranks highest' sat under Multi-Timeframe Confluence but describes Sweep-and-Reclaim, and both 'Where it stands' paragraphs were one block early. The 'missed profits' accounting — '$94.6K missed', '$127K swing', '$158.6K swing', repeated in three places — assumed Jordan would have held every one of those moves to the end. That is the assumption a stopped-out trader most wants to make and the least able to justify. Removed everywhere, with the distinction stated plainly: the $64K is what happened, the rest is what he tells himself happened.

The recovery record ('23 trades, 18 winners, $44K → $89.6K, +104%') and the Pareto claim in his own quote ('20% of setups = 80% profits'). Both gone. What replaces them is the one measurable change: 23 entries where there had been 54, a 60% cut — and the observation that all four new rules subtract entries rather than improving them, which is the whole mechanism.

Nine probability claims: 'Double sweeps are highest probability setups' in the Real Talk and in all three social meta descriptions, 'Pattern #1 (Highest Probability)' as a heading, 'strong absorption (high probability)', 'Expected performance: Moderate to high probability' twice, 'High probability reversal', 'Extreme reversal probability', 'Highest-conviction long setup', and the takeaway calling the double sweep 'the highest-probability pattern'. 'clears 4H + 15m stops = $50M+ institutional flow' — an invented dollar figure for something not visible from outside. Replaced with the statement that no figure can honestly be put on it.

Two sections titled '⚡ Quick Wins for Tomorrow' in one lesson. The second is a review exercise, not a quick win, and the lesson had no practice section at all — retitled 'Practice: Classify Last Week's Sweeps'.

28-janus-atlas-advanced.summary: The double-sweep idea is genuinely worth the lesson: the first sweep takes the obvious stops, the bounce creates a new layer of them, and the second sweep takes both — which explains why a trader can be right about the level and still be stopped out twice before the move. Jordan's case study is unusually good at making that concrete, because the failure is not 'he was wrong', it is 'he was early in a specific, repeatable way, 47 times out of 54'. The three execution frameworks are correctly ranked by how much confirmation each demands, and the 'Common Janus Mistakes' section concedes that not all sweeps reverse.

29-plutus-flow-mastery.notes: This lesson had the densest concentration of invented statistics found in the audit so far: nine fabricated rates and five counterfactual dollar figures on one page, alongside a case study whose own arithmetic is exact. The two coexisting is the pattern the whole audit keeps finding — the careful work and the invented work sit in the same document, and the invented parts are always the ones making a claim about how well the method pays.
29-plutus-flow-mastery.summary: The central distinction is a real one and the lesson is built entirely around it: a POC level is a static snapshot, POC migration is a direction, and reading the first while ignoring the second is what separates the two composites. Jordan's five-day journal is the strongest piece of evidence in the intermediate tier so far — every trade's R and dollar figure reconciles exactly against the stated variable risk (2% for A-grade, 1% for the single B-grade loser), so a reader who checks the arithmetic finds it holds, including on the losing Wednesday. Brandon's twelve-trade disaster is genuinely diagnostic rather than cautionary decoration: each loss maps onto a specific misreading, and the five rules that follow are stated as things that remove entries.
