30-volume-oracle-regimes.notes: Nine of this lesson's numbers were invented and its single hardest fact — Marcus's loss — reconciles exactly. The pattern holds: the fabrications cluster on claims about how well the method pays, never on the arithmetic of how it fails.
30-volume-oracle-regimes.summary: The premise is one of the few in the corpus that survives contact with reality: a strategy is not a thing that works or doesn't, it is a thing that fits some conditions and not others, and 'my strategy stopped working' almost always means the conditions changed. The lesson is structured well around that — three regimes, four detection inputs with numeric thresholds a reader can actually check on a chart (ADX 20/25, VIX 25, ATR 3-5x), and a strategy for each. The five 'Regime Blindness Patterns' are the strongest section: each is a symptom the reader can recognise in their own behaviour, paired with a cause and a specific instruction, and PATTERN 5 ('I'm a breakout trader') correctly identifies the identity trap underneath the whole failure mode.

fixed: Rachel's disaster was dated to Feb 5, 2024, a real session that did not do what the story needs it to do — the Nasdaq closed roughly flat that day. Same defect as the Tesla stop hunt in lesson 23. The date is gone, with the reason stated in the text: she is a composite, and pinning a composite to a real session invites the reader to look it up and find a day that did not do this.

The recovery record, 'Results: 61% win rate, +$14,800, max DD 4.2% (vs 12%)', and its echo in the takeaways, 'Recovery: +$14.8K (19.8% gain) with proper diversification'. The stress test around it survives, because a modelled loss computed from a stated allocation is a calculation the reader can redo; a six-month return is not. The text now says which of the two it is.

The takeaway heading 'Real-world case studies prove the pattern' — Rachel is explicitly labelled a composite four paragraphs above it. Replaced with 'The failure mode is the evidence, and it is arithmetic', and the bullet under it now shows the arithmetic: 8 positions at 1.5% is 12% heat, and 12% is exactly what she lost.

'Even A-grade setups fail 30-40% of the time' — an invented failure rate doing real work in the argument. Replaced with the point it was there to make: A-grade setups fail often enough that several failing on the same day is ordinary, and five of them is 10% heat on that ordinary day.

Two absolute claims: 'This rule alone will prevent catastrophic drawdowns' and 'Keep portfolio heat at 6-8% ... to survive black swan events'. Both now say what the cap actually does rather than promising survival.

'Real Example: Monthly Rebalancing in Action' retitled 'Worked Example' — it is a constructed illustration, not a real account. Its numbers stay untouched, because they are checkable: 38% x 15% = 5.7%, 30% x 15% = 4.5%, and the 1.2% difference is $1,200 on $100K.

The closing line 'Professionals survive market crashes' — replaced with what the lesson actually establishes: the difference shows up on the one day a year when every position turns out to have been the same position.
31-portfolio-construction.kept: Rachel's disaster in full and its arithmetic, which reconciles exactly: 8 positions, 1.5% each, 12% heat, -$10,200 on $85,000 is -12%, and $85,000 - $10,200 = the $74,800 stated. The stress test on the rebuilt portfolio, relabelled as the calculation it is. The Kelly section's expectancy worked examples, whose arithmetic also checks out (0.6x3 - 0.4x1 = +1.4R; 0.5x2 - 0.5x1 = +0.5R) and which correctly insists that neither win rate nor payoff ratio alone is edge. The quiz explanation's 8 x 1.75% = 14%.
31-portfolio-construction.notes: Graded S on 'worth the time' — this is the lesson most likely to change a reader's behaviour on the day they read it, because the failure it describes is one nearly every retail trader has had and almost none has named. The defects were confined to the composite's outcomes and one invented failure rate; the load-bearing arithmetic was already sound throughout.
31-portfolio-construction.summary: This is one of the most useful lessons in the tier, because the thing it teaches is arithmetic and the arithmetic is right. Four positions at 2% risk is 8% total only if they are four different bets; if they all move together it is one 8% bet wearing four names, and a reader who takes nothing else away has still learned something that will change what they do. The 6-8% heat rule is stated as a cap on what being wrong all at once costs, not as a way of being right more often. The correlation section gives the reader a method rather than a rule of thumb — export 30 days of closes, compute daily returns, run CORREL(), colour the matrix — which is unusually concrete for this curriculum, and the reference pairs (SPY/QQQ 0.95, SPY/Gold 0.10-0.30, SPY/VIX -0.80) are close enough to right that a reader who checks them will find the method works.

fixed: The practice exercise instructed readers to 'use the validation scorecard from the template (8 categories, 60 points max)' and to score 50-60 to proceed. No such scorecard existed anywhere on the site — the phrase appears nowhere else in the codebase. The lesson's single most actionable step pointed at nothing. Built the scorecard from the eight checks the lesson already teaches (data split, optimisation restraint, cost modelling, look-ahead, out-of-sample degradation, walk-forward consistency, sample size, breadth), each scored 0-5 for 40 points, with thresholds. Chris's strategy scores 2 out of 40 on it, which is stated, and is the point.

Expectancy and Sharpe thresholds miscalibrated upward throughout, in a lesson whose entire subject is miscalibration. The red flag list warned only above +5R expectancy; a quiz called a +1.2R expectancy 'still profitable but barely'; another prescribed trading live only if expectancy stayed above +1.5R; a third called Sharpe 1.5-2.5 'realistic'. Taken together these tell a reader that a genuinely excellent system is marginal. Recalibrated: above +0.5R needs an explanation, above +1R almost always means a broken execution assumption — and the lesson now points at its own case study, whose 'holy grail' backtest was +1.3R, to make the point stick.

'Why 90% of backtests fail when taken live' — an invented statistic in the opening promise. Replaced with the claim the lesson actually proves: a backtest can be arithmetically correct and still describe a strategy nobody can trade.

Three unsourced magnitudes: 'your backtest is probably 20-40% too optimistic', 'survivorship bias inflates backtest results by 20-50%', and 'excluding 200+ stocks that got delisted/bankrupted'. The last is also wrong on the facts — index turnover is real but most departures are acquisitions or size-band exits, not bankruptcies. All three now describe the mechanism and its direction and hand the magnitude back to the reader's own calculation, which is what the rest of the lesson demands anyway.

The fantasy backtest's headline, '+$40,600 (+406%)', could not be reconciled with anything else in the table until you guessed the account size. It reconciles exactly on a $10,000 test account at 2% risk: 156 trades x 1.3R x $200 = $40,560, and $40,600 on $10,000 is 406%. That is now stated in the row label, so the whole table is checkable rather than only most of it.
32-backtesting-reality.kept: The seven-category cost autopsy in full, including every input, because every one of them can be recomputed. Chris's optimisation process (50 EMA periods x 20 ATR multipliers x 15 targets = 15,000 combinations), which is the mechanism of the failure. The in-sample/out-of-sample comparison and its 71% degradation. The walk-forward framework. The four ways backtests lie, each with a concrete example and a fix.
32-backtesting-reality.notes: The first S grade in the intermediate tier. What earns it is not that the lesson is free of defects — it had five — but that its central artefact does the thing the rest of the curriculum needed doing to it: takes an impressive-looking performance record and shows, arithmetically, where the impression came from. The defects were at the edges: a dangling reference, upward-drifting thresholds, and three round numbers with nothing behind them.
32-backtesting-reality.summary: This is the best lesson in the curriculum so far, and it is best precisely where the rest of the corpus has been weakest: it demolishes a fabricated performance record, in public, line by line, and shows its working. Chris's 'perfect' backtest is +1.3R expectancy, 4.9 profit factor, 67% win rate, +406% over two years. The lesson then accounts for every dollar of the gap between that and the -$8,400 he actually lost, in seven categories, and lands within $250 of the real figure. Every line of that accounting is checkable: 0.08% slippage on $25K over 37 round trips is $1,480; $0.65 per contract on 20 contracts over 37 round trips is $962; five missed winners at 1.8R less three avoided losers at 1.3R is -5.1R, which at $500 per R is $2,550. A reader who redoes the arithmetic finds it holds. The out-of-sample section then shows what would have caught it in advance, with the degradation figure (2023 expectancy 29% of 2022) doing the work.

fixed: Two genuine mathematical errors in the Risk of Ruin section, which is the section a reader is most likely to take on trust. A 50% win rate at 1:1 was given a Risk of Ruin of '~50%'; with no edge, gambler's ruin is certain — the correct figure is 100%, and it is a far better teaching point than the wrong one. And the practice exercise put Trader A's Risk of Ruin at '~40%' with the two traders '40x' apart; the formula the lesson itself supplies gives 13.4% and 0.004%, which is a factor of about 3,000. Both corrected. The exercise now asks the reader to compute the ratio rather than handing them a wrong one.

The RoR formula's exponent was labelled 'Max Trades' and glossed as 'max consecutive losses before ruin', which reads as the probability of a losing streak rather than the probability of ever going broke. It is units of capital — how many full-size losses fit in the account — and the lesson now says so, states the 1:1 payoff assumption the formula rests on, and draws out the two consequences: halving risk squares the survival odds, and at a 50% win rate the base becomes 1 and the whole expression collapses.

The composite's recovery record: '31 trades, 23 wins, max DD -8.4% vs -69.2% (-88% improvement) ... $15.4K → $27.7K (+79.9% recovery)'. The behavioural half survives — zero protocol violations in 26 weeks, worst week -$510 against -$9,200, worst drawdown 8.4% against 69.2% — because those describe what he did. The return does not. What replaces it is the arithmetic that actually justifies the whole lesson: recovering from a 69.2% drawdown requires a 225% gain.

Two counterfactuals. 'The math: reducing at -15% would have saved him $20K+' — not calculable, because the trades he took at full size are not the trades he would have taken at half size. And in his own quote, 'Those rules saved me from blowing the remaining $15K'. Both replaced; the quote now says the honest version, that he cannot know what he would have done without them. The checkable comparison stays: +17.6% to recover from -15%, +225% from -69.2%.

'Prop firms auto-liquidate at 8%', asserted three times as though it were a fact about portfolio heat. Funded-trading firms impose drawdown limits, not heat limits, and the thresholds vary widely between firms. Replaced with what is true and is the actual point: every such firm enforces some hard limit and closes you at it, and a limit you cannot override is worth more than a limit you intend to respect.
'This one check prevents 90% of account blowups' in the Quick Wins — an invented rate attached to an otherwise excellent two-minute instruction. The instruction stands on its own.
33-advanced-risk-management.kept: Kevin's descent in full, week by week, including tripling down on BTC at -52%. The Kelly derivation and both worked examples, whose arithmetic checks out ((0.6x450 - 0.4x250)/450 = 0.378; (0.6x2 - 0.4)/2 = 0.40). The daily, pre-trade and post-trade checklists. The four practice scenarios. The cost-tracking quiz, which is the only place in the tier that makes a reader reconcile a broker statement against their own P&L and find a $200 gap.
33-advanced-risk-management.notes: This is the first lesson in the audit whose defects included real mathematical errors rather than only invented figures, and both were in the section with the most authority — a named formula with worked numbers. The formula itself was right; what was wrong was the label on its exponent and two of the three numbers plugged into it.
33-advanced-risk-management.summary: The three-tier structure is the right way to teach this: per-trade risk, portfolio heat, and drawdown, with the drawdown protocol explicitly overriding the other two. The first quiz question tests exactly that override — heat is fine at 7.5%, drawdown is -15%, and the answer is cut anyway — which is the one place traders reliably get it wrong. The Kelly section is unusually careful, and correct where most treatments are not: it derives full Kelly, refuses it, walks fractional Kelly down, and then makes the point that matters, which is that Kelly is a ceiling rather than a target and you take the lower of it and your per-trade cap. Kevin's disaster reconciles exactly ($34,600 is 69.2% of $50,000, leaving the $15.4K stated) and the escalation is the useful part: he averaged down fourteen times and increased size at -32%.

fixed: A table of win rates and average R for Signal Pilot's own indicators — 'Janus only: 58% WR, 2.3R; Janus + Plutus: 66%, 3.1R; Janus + Plutus + Volume Oracle: 72%, 3.6R' — presented as what a reader's journal would show, and concluding 'Confluence dramatically improves edge'. This is the company publishing performance figures for its own products with nothing behind them, and it is the single worst instance found in the audit. Replaced with the same three-way split as a blank template, plus the reason the blanks are there, plus the trap the exercise walks into: requiring more confluence removes trades, so what is left looks better almost by construction. That is selection, not evidence, and the lesson now says so.

A second fabricated table, 'Performance by R:R', giving win rates by R:R bucket. Replaced with the same bucketing as a template and the observation that actually teaches: the win rate is supposed to fall as the target moves further away, so the column to read is total R, and a bucket can win 40% of the time and still be the best one.

Four extrapolations, each turning a small sample into an annual figure. '30 days x 1 trade/day = +$5,400/month ... a $60K/year leak' from twelve morning trades. 'Over 50 weeks, this saves $25K+' from three FOMO trades. 'Over 12 months = +$13,200 from ONE journal insight' from one month of 47 trades. 'This 10-minute exercise often reveals a $5K-10K annual leak' from five trades. All removed; the within-sample arithmetic that the reader can check is kept in every case.

'Week 2: 4 FOMO urges, skipped all 4, saved ~$1,300 in losses' — the counterfactual in its purest form, and the mirror image of the missed-profits fallacy this curriculum has been removing everywhere else. A skipped trade has no result. The lesson now says exactly that, names the symmetry with traders who credit themselves for profits they imagine they missed, and tells the reader to track compliance rather than savings.

Morgan's after-record, stated twice: 'monthly income went from $1,367 to $4,160 by closing the blind spot' and 'tripling it by trading LESS'. What replaces it is the change that can be reported honestly — Friday went from the most-traded day of the week to the least — and the observation that the intervention needed no strategy change, no new indicator, and no profit figure attached to be worth doing.

'If they'd simply skipped Fridays, their 6-month return would have been +16.9% instead of +8.2%' restated as what it actually is: Monday to Thursday, on their own, came to +16.9%. Same number, no counterfactual.
34-trade-journal-mastery.kept: Morgan's full day-of-week breakdown, the 107% figure, and the behavioural root cause. Every piece of within-sample arithmetic in the three knowledge-check questions, all of which reconciles (12 x $180 = $2,160; 18 x -$95 = -$1,710; $4,200/20 = $210; -$1,100/15 = -$73; $1,680/12 = $140; $5,880 - $4,780 = $1,100 = +23%). The five-mistake taxonomy and the confluence scoring rubric.
34-trade-journal-mastery.notes: This lesson was teaching readers to be rigorous with their own data while modelling the opposite: two fabricated performance tables, four annualised extrapolations, one counterfactual saving, and one composite income record. The fix in every case was the same move the lesson already recommends elsewhere — report what the sample shows, and stop there.
34-trade-journal-mastery.summary: The core argument is right and is made well: a journal is not a diary, it is a dataset, and its value comes entirely from segmenting it. Morgan's Friday leak is the best illustration of that idea in the corpus — the account was up 8.2% over six months, Monday to Thursday was up 16.9%, and the Friday losses came to 107% of everything the other four days had made. The reader can check that: 8,740 divided by 8,200 is 106.6%. And the cause the journal exposes is behavioural rather than market-related (51 trades on Fridays, the most of any day, forced to 'end the week green'), which is the whole point — the fix was a rule about one day of the week, not a new strategy. The Quick Wins are unusually well judged: six columns, thirty seconds a trade, a Sunday reminder.

fixed: Both composites carried recovery records. Rachel: '29 trades, 25 of them winners, 2.4:1 R:R, +$41K'. Michael: three week-blocks at +$3,200, +$4,800 and +$18,700, then 'Recovered $26,700 of the $47K loss, 23 winners in 28 trades against 14 in 43 before'. Removed in both cases, keeping the counts that describe behaviour rather than outcome: 29 trades where there had been 82, 28 where there had been 43, zero stop moves, zero revenge trades, 53 setups the checklist stopped her taking.

The $18K stop-discipline figure was stated as a saving three times ('NEVER moving stops saved $18K', 'she moved stops 0 times and saved approximately $18,000', and a quiz question built entirely on it). A saving from trades not taken is unknowable — but the same arithmetic run backwards is entirely sound, because those 34 stop moves DID happen and each one has a measurable cost. Reframed throughout as $17,850 incurred rather than $18,000 saved, and Q5 rewritten to ask what the habit cost and how you know, which turns a counterfactual question into a checkable one.
The same reframe applied to Michael: 'Stop discipline saved $16,200' became 'moving stops had cost him $16,200', which is nine moves x $1,800 and reconciles exactly.

'This 30-min ritual prevents 80% of bad trades', stated twice — an invented rate. Replaced with why the ritual works at all: it fixes your bias before the market gives you a reason to want a different one.

Three extrapolations. 'Over 50 weeks: -$600/week from rushed entries = -$30,000/year' from a single illustrative trade. And in the session-splitting question, an elaborate chain — '12 morning trades/15 days = 0.8/day x 20 days = 16 trades x $390 = +$6,240/month ... +$4,000/month (+$48K/year)' — built on twelve observed trades. Both replaced with what the sample does establish, which is that one session is paying for the other, and with the reason the forecast is not available: the mornings that produced those trades were the mornings that happened to offer setups.
'skip trade, saved $500 loss' in the Quick Wins — replaced with the observation that matters more than the imagined saving: three checklist items said no and you were about to click anyway.
'3-5 high-probability candidates daily' from the scanner output — the scanner filters on four stated criteria and cannot speak to probability. Now 'candidates that meet every criterion'.
35-professional-operations.kept: Both disasters in full, including every diagnostic detail: Rachel's 9:45 wake-up, 34 stop moves, 27 revenge trades and 26% win rate; Michael's 11-of-11 losses before 10:30, his eight no-confluence losses, and his nine stop moves. The complete pre-market, session and post-market phases with their timings. The workspace layouts, the automation tools, the four circuit breakers, and the weekly and monthly routines.
35-professional-operations.notes: The pattern in this lesson is worth naming because it recurs across the tier: the same number is honest in one direction and fabricated in the other. What a bad habit cost is arithmetic on trades that happened. What a good rule saved is a guess about trades that did not. This lesson had the figure pointing the wrong way in five places; it now points the right way, and is stronger for it, because $17,850 of a $73,000 loss traceable to one repeated action is a more useful fact than a promise about the future.
35-professional-operations.summary: The claim this lesson makes is unusual for the genre and it is right: the thing separating two traders with identical strategies is often not the strategy at all. Both composites lose large sums while knowing exactly what a good setup looks like — Rachel woke at 9:45 for a 9:30 open and entered at daily resistance without ever checking it; Michael's backtests were profitable and he moved his stop nine times. The remedy is correspondingly unglamorous and specific: a 30-minute pre-market sequence with five named steps, a five-item entry checklist small enough to tape to a monitor, a 15-minute post-market review, and four circuit breakers. The single best thing in the lesson is a piece of arithmetic: moving a stop 34 times, each move turning a planned -$1,050 into a realised -$1,575, is $525 x 34 = $17,850 — a quarter of the whole disaster, from one habit, and the reader can verify every step of it.

fixed: The lesson defined the '@T' sale condition as 'Form T = late report = dark pool', repeated it in eleven places, built a Time & Sales filter instruction on it, and made it the subject of a quiz question. This is wrong. The T condition marks a trade executed outside regular market hours; it appears on pre-market and after-hours prints of every size and says nothing about whether a trade was internalised or crossed in an ATS. The identifier is the exchange code, 'D'. A reader following the old instruction would have filtered their tape down to extended-hours odd lots and concluded dark pools were full of 200-share trades. Corrected throughout, with the folklore named as folklore.

A second, contradictory error alongside it: 'delayed reporting: may appear 10 seconds to 30 minutes after actual execution', stated twice, while two other passages correctly said trades must be reported within 10 seconds. The 10-second rule is the true one; the half-hour delay is not a thing.

'40% of equity volume trades in dark pools', asserted four times — and then contradicted by the lesson's own Part 4, which correctly says most of that off-exchange share is wholesaler internalisation of retail orders, i.e. explicitly not dark pools. Rewritten to separate the two, because the distinction is the whole basis for calling one of them signal and the other noise.

'Citadel sees YOUR order before it's executed, can trade ahead (legal but controversial)' — trading ahead of a customer order is prohibited, and describing it as legal about a named firm is both wrong and unfair. Replaced with the argument people actually have about PFOF: whether a firm that sees most of the retail tape in aggregate gains an advantage from knowing its shape. The '$0.002/share' PFOF rate was also roughly an order of magnitude high for equities; corrected, with the note that options pay far more, which is the real reason brokers court that flow.

The 'Real Trade Example (September 2023)' was dated onto a calendar that refutes it: it places trades on September 3rd, a Sunday, and September 4th, Labor Day, and has SPY making new highs at $460 during a month in which SPY fell from about $451 to about $423. Converted to a numbered-day worked example, with the reason stated in the text.

Tyler's composite carried the same problem — 'October 15th' was a Sunday, and SPY was near $434 and falling on the October 12th the story needs at $459 — plus a quantified after-record ('Profit: $14,200 on 1,000 shares') and a testimonial. Dates removed, result removed, and the contrast that matters kept: the first short was taken because an indicator said the market had gone up a lot, the second because size was leaving while price went up.

Both trades quoted returns on margin at '10x leverage' — leverage not available on US equities to retail, where Reg T gives 2x overnight and 4x intraday. Replaced with R. The lesson now makes the point explicitly: dividing a fixed profit by a margin figure lets you print any percentage you like by choosing the denominator, which is why a return-on-margin claim should always prompt the question.
'Adds 5-8% to win rate' for the price/DIX divergence, and two 'high-probability' labels.
36-dark-pool-indicators.kept: The routing walkthrough, the block-size thresholds by instrument, the four print patterns, the DIX bands, and the complete long setup with its five requirements. The absorption logic in Q5, which is the subtlest idea in the lesson and is correctly reasoned.
36-dark-pool-indicators.notes: Graded B rather than A because the defects were factual rather than promotional, and because two of them were instructions. Everything else in the audit so far has involved numbers that were too flattering; this lesson also had mechanics that were simply wrong, and a reader who trusted them would have spent weeks filtering the wrong column. The corrections are all in the direction of what the tape actually does.
36-dark-pool-indicators.summary: The subject is real and the framing is right: a large share of US equity volume prints away from lit books, the prints surface on the tape seconds later, and the difference between price making new highs and size quietly leaving is a genuine thing to look at. The mechanics section is the best part — how an order is routed, why an institution wants the midpoint, why a 500,000-share fill would be front-run if it appeared on a public book. The block-size table scaled by instrument liquidity is a good piece of thinking. But this lesson carried more factual errors than any other audited so far, and they were not decorative: two of them told the reader to do something that does not work.

fixed: The gamma sign was inverted. 'Positive GEX above price = dealers buy rallies (amplifies moves)' — it is the opposite. Long-gamma dealers sell into strength and buy into weakness, which compresses the range; the squeeze that ran Brandon over is a NEGATIVE gamma phenomenon. The lesson said this correctly elsewhere and contradicted itself here, in the framework paragraph, in the checklist, and in the Q5 explanation. A reader who learned the rule from the wrong passage would look for a squeeze in exactly the regime that suppresses one. Corrected in all three places, with the confusion named so the reader can spot it in other people's writing.

The missing caveat that makes 'never fight big flow' safe to hold. A large call print is not proof anybody is bullish: it can be one leg of a spread, an overwrite against stock already owned, a hedge on a short, or a dealer on the other side of all of them. The tape shows size and aggression, never the position the trade belongs to. Added before the recovery system, and made the subject of the rewritten Q4 — because the honest reading (hedging demand is certain, intent is invisible) is both more useful and more defensible than the version the lesson had.

Five invented hit rates: 'moves toward strike ~68% of time', 'P/C >1.5 precedes bounces ~72% within 1-5 days', 'moves toward max pain 64%', 'win rate OpEx days: ~60-65%', and '3-way confluence = 70-80% win rate'. Each removed and replaced with what is actually known — including, for pinning, that the academic work finds it far more clearly in single names with concentrated open interest than in an index ETF traded in SPY's size.

Brandon's composite after-record, in four places: the recovery line ('Gained $53K in 10 weeks, 51% recovery'), three constructed winning trades presented as the method working, the Results block, and — the worst of them — as the correct answer to Q4, which had to be rewritten around a real question. The before-record stays: 27 trades, 3 winners, -$96K is a disaster he lived, and it is the part that teaches.

Two absolutes: 'P/C extreme + structure hold = high-probability bottom' and 'this demonstrates why you NEVER fight massive institutional options flow'. The second replaced with the accurate version — big flow is not always right, it just creates hedging you have to trade against as well as the position itself.
37-options-order-flow.kept: The UOA screen and its three filters, the GEX map and zero-gamma level, the put/call sentiment bands, the max-pain and pinning mechanics, the confluence worked example with its R arithmetic, and Brandon's blowup in full.
37-options-order-flow.notes: Graded B for the same reason as 36: the defect was factual, not merely promotional, and it sat in the mechanic the lesson exists to teach. Everything downstream of the correction is stronger — the hedging argument survives on its own without the win rates that were propping it up, and the rewritten Q4 now tests the distinction between what flow proves and what it only suggests, which is the single most useful thing in the lesson.
37-options-order-flow.summary: The premise is sound and unusually well chosen for an equity trader: options flow matters to you not because it reveals what an institution believes, but because whoever sold those contracts has to hedge them in the underlying, and that hedging is buying and selling you will trade against whether you looked at it or not. The unusual-activity screen (volume against open interest, premium size, execution at the ask), the gamma-exposure map, put/call extremes and max pain are the right four things to teach, and Brandon's NVDA blowup is a genuinely good disaster: he was short into $35M of call flow and the dealers hedging it, and he had accounted for neither. But the lesson stated its own central mechanic backwards in two places, and one of those was the answer to a quiz question.

fixed: 'YOUR profit is someone else's loss. That makes trading a zero-sum game' — the lesson's opening premise, and false as stated. Equities as a whole are not zero-sum; futures are zero-sum before costs and negative-sum after. What is close to zero-sum is short-horizon trading against other short-horizon traders, which is exactly what the lesson is about, so the argument survives intact once stated precisely.

The manipulation story, which ran through the whole lesson: institutions 'sweep stops' as a deliberate 'dominant strategy'. Deliberately pressing price to trigger stops rather than to trade at those prices is manipulation and is prosecuted. The observable phenomenon needs no such story: stops cluster below the obvious level because that is where every course puts them, and a buyer who needs size wants to be filled where supply is. Same conclusion, no conspiracy, and a reader who learns the second version will not spend their career looking for villains. The actionable advice is unchanged.

'Institutions can coordinate legally (through prime brokerage relationships, shared research, dark pool order flow visibility)' with a supporting list — prime brokers sharing client order-flow patterns is what information barriers exist to prevent, and dark pools are dark by construction: you cannot see other participants' resting orders in one. Also 'retail traders can't coordinate (illegal to collude)' — agreeing where to put stops would not be illegal, it is merely impossible to arrange. Replaced with how a large participant actually infers where liquidity sits, which needs no coordination at all and makes the coordination-failure point better.

Part 2 was titled 'Prisoner's Dilemma in Liquidity Provision' and then presented a stop-placement decision matrix that is not a prisoner's dilemma — there is no cooperative option for you and a large buyer to abandon. Named plainly, in a lesson about game theory, and pointed at the place where the structure genuinely does appear.

Q2's answer had market makers 'committing to provide liquidity regardless'. They widen and step back when adverse selection rises, which is exactly why spreads blow out in a panic; they are paid to carry the risk, not sworn to ignore it. Rewritten, including what a designated market maker's quoting obligation actually guarantees.

Eight invented figures: '60-70% vs 40-45%' win rates for the two strategies, '60-70% of reversals have sweeps' (twice), '80% place stops just below support' (twice), 'win rate jumps to 70%+', 'you survive 70% more sweeps', and a 30% failure rate the exercise never supplied. The 65% in the expected-value calculation was kept as a stated assumption, with the arithmetic run at 50%, 40% and the 37.5% break-even so the reader can see how fast the edge dies.

'Real Example: ES Futures Support Sweep (June 2024)' — constructed minute by minute, and ES was nowhere near 5250 that June. Converted to an undated worked example, with the unobservable '10,000+ retail longs with stops at 5245-5248' replaced by what a chart actually shows, and two headline totals ($9M-11.5M, $12.5M) removed: the contract count they multiply is not observable.

Sarah's after-record ('18 trades, 13 winners, $14,150 in 2 months') and her testimonial. Her three months of false stop-outs stay — 23 stops at $750 is arithmetic on trades that happened, and it is the part that teaches.
38-game-theory-trading.kept: The Nash equilibrium framing of current price, the support-level payoff matrix (now labelled as illustrative ranks), the three levels of reasoning, the Level 3 stop framework and its TSLA worked calculation, all three practice exercises with their arithmetic, the mixed-strategy section, and the adversarial-thinking framework, which is the cleanest statement of the lesson's idea.
38-game-theory-trading.notes: Graded B for the same reason as 36 and 37: the errors were factual and structural rather than merely promotional, and one of them was the lesson's opening sentence. But this is the lesson whose corrections improved it most. The conspiratorial version of stop-hunting is emotionally satisfying and analytically useless; the resting-order version explains the same tape, predicts the same behaviour, and tells the reader what to do about it. Every number in the lesson was already correct, which made it unusually easy to fix — the problem was never the arithmetic.
38-game-theory-trading.summary: The best-conceived lesson in the tier and, before the corrections, one of the most over-claimed. The core idea is genuinely valuable and rare in trading education: your stop is not a private decision, it is a move in a game where the other side knows what traders like you typically do. The three levels of reasoning (what will price do / what will traders do / what will they think traders do) are the Keynesian beauty contest applied correctly. The Level 3 stop framework — place the stop where the thesis is wrong, plus a volatility buffer, rather than at the level everyone can see — is the single most actionable idea in the intermediate tier, and every piece of arithmetic supporting it checks out, which after thirty-seven lessons is worth saying out loud. What was wrong was the story the lesson told about why sweeps happen.

fixed: The forced-unwind myth, throughout. A dealer short calls that finish in the money does not sell the hedge — the calls are exercised and the hedge is DELIVERED. Calls that finish out of the money see their hedge run off as delta decays, which follows the move rather than causing it. And the flow is not one-directional: a dealer short puts that expire worthless has to buy back short stock at the same moment. Replaced with what actually happens, plus the reason it matters: 'buy puts at 3 PM on OpEx Friday' requires knowing which way price leaves the strike before the flow tells you anything, which is the whole problem.

A direct internal contradiction. Part 1 says dealers short options amplify moves (buy higher, sell lower); Part 3's charm section runs that exact mechanic and concludes 'price pins to the strike'. Those are opposite outcomes. Pinning requires dealers to be LONG gamma at the strike; short gamma pushes price away. Both signs now stated, with the research finding noted: expiration clustering shows up where market makers are net long the strike and anti-clustering where they are net short.

The definition of max pain — 'the strike where the most options expire worthless, maximum profit for market makers' — is wrong twice. It is the strike minimising total intrinsic payout (a different number, since cheap and expensive contracts do not weigh the same), and market makers are hedged and roughly flat, not the net writers. Corrected, and the section headed 'How to Calculate Max Pain', which had a heading and no body at all, now has the five-step calculation with a worked fragment and a statement of the two things it cannot tell you.

The vanna table gave one sign for 'calls' when vanna changes sign across the strike, and concluded that falling IV is bearish. In index books, where customers are net buyers of downside puts, falling IV releases dealers from short stock hedges — this is the vanna tailwind that lifts markets after an event passes. The lesson's trade instruction, 'short SPY when VIX drops below 20', was therefore backwards on a well-documented relationship. Removed with the reasoning shown.

The Volmageddon timeline: the jobs report was Friday 2 February, not 1 PM on Monday the 5th; the VIX move (17.31 to 37.32, about +116%) was a full day, not 2.5 hours; VIX above 50 was the following morning; XIV's indicative value fell about 96%, not 100%. Also 'VIX spikes to 30-60 two or three times per year' — in most calendar years since 1990 it does not happen at all.

The opening paragraph, which multiplied 200,000 contracts by full notional to get a $9 billion hedge (at 0.50 delta it is about $4.5 billion) and assumed dealers were short all of them. That assumption — open interest equals dealer short position — ran silently through every figure in the lesson and is now stated wherever it is used.

'Citadel is now delta-neutral (profit from theta decay)' — a delta-hedged short call earns theta and pays gamma, and only makes money if realised volatility comes in under implied. The half that can bankrupt you was missing.

The put/call row in the dealer-positioning table gave the identical reading — 'dealers short gamma' — for both a high and a low ratio, which cannot be a signal. GME's dealer hedge figures ('150M+ shares, 3x the float') were invented and impossible, exceeding shares outstanding; removed rather than guessed at. Tool subscription prices removed, with the point that every gamma service is running a model, not reporting data.

Both composites' after-records: Kyle's recovery trade and 12-trade, 75% record; Sarah's TSLA trade, +$60K, and 14-trade, 78.6%, +$184.3K record; both testimonials; and the trailing recovery line on Sarah's quiz card. The disasters stay — $67,200 in 45 minutes and $96,000 in six hours are what the lesson is for.

The playbook: two invented win rates (65% monthly, 68% zero-day), four constructed winning example trades, and the recommendation to sell a naked at-the-money straddle on expiration day. That last one is the most dangerous instruction in the audited curriculum so far: undefined maximum loss, assignment risk in exactly the scenario the trade is built on, and a high win rate offered as the reason to take it.
39-options-market-microstructure.kept: The delta-hedging walkthrough and its arithmetic, gamma as the rate of change of delta, the GME price path (public record), the charm mechanics, the long/short gamma regime distinction in Part 6, the DIX and GEX descriptions, and all three knowledge-check questions, whose correct answers survive with corrected explanations.
39-options-market-microstructure.notes: Graded C because the defect was structural rather than local. In lessons 36 to 38 the actionable advice survived correction; here the primary instruction — never buy calls in the last hour because dealers must dump — rested on a mechanism that does not work as described, and its mirror image ('buy puts instead, OpEx is an ATM') was offered as the recovery lesson in both case studies. The honest version of what happened to Kyle and Sarah is simpler and better: they bought same-day options and needed the market to move a specific distance within hours. That is a complete explanation, it needs no villain, and it generalises. The lesson is now built on it.
39-options-market-microstructure.summary: The most ambitious lesson in the tier and the first to earn a C. Its subject is real and under-taught: dealer hedging is mechanical, it is large, and it does move the underlying. The delta-hedging walkthrough is genuinely good — every figure in it checks out — and the treatment of gamma, charm and vanna as distinct forces is more than most retail material attempts. But the lesson's central claim was that dealers are OBLIGED to liquidate billions of dollars of stock into the close on expiration Friday, and that claim is false. It appeared in six places, it was the stated cause of both case-study losses, it was the correct answer to both case-study quizzes, it drove the 'never buy calls after 3 PM' rule, and it was the premise of the entire nine-part trading playbook. Correcting it meant rewriting the spine.
